read: partial: main text pp. 1-9 in full (abstract, introduction, repository, crowdsourcing and annotation, pipeline, benchmark, results, ablations, related work, conclusion, limitations; tables read for their headline rows); appendix A.1-A.2 (p. 11) and A.8-A.9 (p. 13) read; remaining appendix tables and figures not read
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2310.07018v1, 10 Oct 2023 (p. 1); the text shows no venue (it has an ACL-style Limitations section, p. 9)
what_it_is: A repository, generation pipeline and benchmark for LLMs' qualitative physical reasoning about everyday objects (p. 1-2). Crowd workers rated 700+ household objects, drawn from 3D object datasets and mapped to WordNet, on 8 physical attributes (elasticity, stiffness, surface smoothness, surface hardness, softness, brittleness, malleability, sharpness) on a 3-point scale, with at least four annotators per pair and an agreement filter, giving 2,800 object-attribute pairs (p. 1-3). Templates filled from this repository generate 160K multiple-choice and Boolean questions in three tracks: foundational attribute comprehension, explicit application and implicit everyday scenarios (p. 4). Models from Flan-T5 to GPT-4 are scored by agreement with the human majority or by accuracy; GPT-4 leads but trails human agreement on attribute questions (p. 5-6).
domain: physical commonsense: qualitative physical attributes of everyday household objects, motivated by robotic manipulation (p. 1-2, p. 8)
size: 160K questions in 3 tracks; repository of 2,800 object-attribute pairs over 700+ objects and 8 attributes (p. 1-2, p. 4); 20,000+ crowd annotations (p. 3); ten model entries in Tables 3-4 (p. 5-6)
source_of_items: generated from templates filled from a crowd-sourced object-attribute repository; objects from Objaverse, YCB, Google Scanned Objects and Amazon Berkeley Objects mapped to WordNet synsets (p. 2-4); Track 3 scenarios hand-designed (p. 11)
instances: generated (160K pre-generated questions from templates; the pipeline can generate further customised questions, p. 1, p. 3)
has_gold_traces: no: each question has a single correct option derived from the filtered crowd labels; there are no solutions or reasoning steps
evaluation: multiple choice (up to four options, exactly one correct) and Boolean: Track 1 by agreement with the human majority weighted by inter-annotator agreement, Tracks 2-3 by accuracy (p. 4-5; formulas p. 11)
human_validation: Labels: 3-point Likert annotations, at least four annotators per object-attribute pair, 20,000+ annotations; pairs kept only at agreement of at least 0.75 (three of four) and with extreme ratings (p. 3). Pilot studies on 5% of objects tuned the question format and attribute list (p. 2). The authors note possible crowdsourcing errors (p. 9). No validation of the generated questions or the scoring beyond this filtering is reported.

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: Within S-P1, 'qualitative' is accurate for this paper: NEWTON asks about qualitative attributes such as elasticity, brittleness and softness of everyday objects, as three-option, Boolean or multiple-choice questions with no calculation (p. 2, p. 4). The paragraph's framing is not: NEWTON is not a physical-sciences or 'theoretical physics' benchmark (S-P2) but a physical-commonsense benchmark about household objects, built from crowd-sourced labels and motivated by robotic manipulation (p. 1-3, p. 8), so for this paper S-P2 contradicts the source. The sentence also omits that NEWTON's 160K questions are generated by filling templates and that its pipeline can generate more (p. 1, p. 3-4), which bears on EngTrace's claim to template generation (S-I2).

suggested_wording: NEWTON (Wang et al., 2023) fills templates from crowd-sourced object-attribute labels to generate 160K multiple-choice questions on the qualitative physical properties of everyday objects.
facts_to_cite: A repository of 2,800 object-attribute pairs, crowd-sourced for 700+ household objects and 8 physical attributes (p. 1-2).
Labels come from a 3-point Likert task with at least four annotators per pair (20,000+ annotations), kept only at agreement of at least 0.75 (p. 3).

160K questions are generated by filling templates, in three tracks: foundational attribute comprehension, explicit application (Boolean and multiple choice) and implicit scenario-based analysis (p. 4); the pipeline can generate further customised questions (p. 1, p. 3).
Every question is answered by choosing one of at most four options (p. 4).

GPT-4 scores 49.7 agreement on Track 1 against a mean inter-annotator agreement of 84.4 (Table 4, p. 6; the abstract's '50% vs. 84%', p. 1), and 87.7% on the Track 3 scenarios against a 44.5% average over the evaluated models (p. 6).
The motivation is LLM use in physically grounded settings such as robotic manipulation (p. 1, p. 8).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: template-generated items at scale from a validated repository (160K questions, with a pipeline for more, p. 1-4); agreement-based filtering of human labels (p. 3). Lacks: quantitative or multi-step problems; free-response answers (multiple choice and Boolean only, p. 4); gold traces; step-level evaluation; an engineering setting (everyday household objects, p. 2); any evaluator needing validation (scoring is exact match against crowd labels, p. 5, p. 11).
notes: Naming clash: the July rebuttal cites SciBench as 'Wang et al., 2023', the same key this paper has in the May reference list; SciBench's text shows ICML 2024 (its p. 1), so citing that version as Wang et al., 2024 keeps the keys distinct. The abstract's '84%' is mean inter-annotator agreement, not a human solver score (Table 4 caption, p. 6). Objects are '700+' in the text (p. 2-4) and '600+' in Table 2 (p. 5). The May reference list misprints one of four given names (Jia for Jiafei Duan; citation_context_map.md). Of the five papers in this review NEWTON is the weakest fit for an engineering paper and the first to cut if space is short; it is kept here because, with ABench-Physics's numeric variants, it shows that generating physical-reasoning questions from templates predates EngTrace. Confidence is high on the verdict and medium on the recommendation.
